principles.name: One Team
principles.description: Work in alignment: break down silos, share context openly and aim at shared goals. Success is shared, and people show up for each other.
evidence_signals: Shared context with another squad or team without being asked
Resolved a cross-team disagreement through alignment rather than escalation
Credits the team for wins and names own part clearly

principles.name: Human Judgment
principles.description: Make well-considered decisions and take thoughtful risks. People are trusted to decide what to build, own the results, learn from mistakes and grow.
evidence_signals: Made a call without a manager directing them and explains the reasoning
Names the risk taken and how it was limited
Owns a mistake and shows what changed afterwards

principles.name: Make It Happen
principles.description: Bias toward action. Do not wait for ideal conditions; create them, and focus on execution, urgency and results that matter.
evidence_signals: Started work before everything was clear and adjusted along the way
Removed a blocker or created the conditions a project needed
Delivered a concrete result under time pressure

principles.name: Impact over activity
principles.description: From Spotify's culture pages: growth comes from the difference you make and the problems you solve, not hours worked. Outcomes, risks taken and value created count.
evidence_signals: Measures success by user or business outcomes, not effort
Quantifies the result of a project
Chose a harder problem because it mattered more

principles.name: Stay curious
principles.description: From Spotify's culture pages: stay curious, experiment, learn continuously and use new tools, including AI, to improve the work.
evidence_signals: Ran an experiment to learn rather than argue
Picked up a new tool or skill and applied it to real work
Seeks feedback and shows how it changed their approach

question_patterns.pattern: A decision the candidate drove in an autonomous team without a manager telling them what to do
A disagreement with another team or with stakeholders who wanted different things, settled by alignment rather than escalation
A failure, mistake or piece of hard feedback, and what the candidate changed afterwards
A tight deadline or blocked project the candidate still moved to a result
How the candidate helps teammates, shares credit and keeps ego out of team decisions
A project the candidate is proud of, delivered from start to finish: own role, decisions and measured result
Why Spotify, how the candidate uses the product, and how they like to work
Design a streaming, playlist, catalog or search system for hundreds of millions of listeners, with caching, CDN and latency trade-offs
Design or improve a recommendation surface such as a weekly personalized playlist: candidate retrieval, ranking, cold start and evaluation
Walk through debugging a production incident or slow service after a release: triage, data to check, escalation and follow-up
Define goals, a primary metric and guardrails for a Spotify feature such as a personalized playlist or podcast surface
A key metric such as installs or streams fell; find the cause and decide what to do

question_patterns.theme: Improve or design a listening experience
question_patterns.pattern: Improve Spotify or design a new feature for one listener or creator group, prioritize, and test it with an experiment

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to make a product decision when stakeholders wanted different things. What did you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Name the stakeholders and what each wanted, and why both views were reasonable. Show how the candidate shared context, found the shared goal, and used data or a small test to decide. Make the final call and its owner clear, and how the others were brought along. End with the result and the relationship afterwards. Pitfalls: escalating straight away, or a story where one side was simply wrong.

looking_for: How you align people who want different things
Who made the call and why
strong_signals: States each side fairly
Uses data or a small test to decide
Shows the result and the relationship afterwards
watch_outs: A story where the other side was simply wrong

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you drove an important decision without a manager telling you what to do.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Set the scene: an autonomous team, an open question, and why waiting was costly. Show how the candidate gathered input, weighed options and the risks, made the call, and told others. Say what they personally decided, using 'I' for their own actions. Give the outcome and what they would do differently. Pitfalls: vague 'we decided' answers, or waiting for permission.

looking_for: Whether you act with autonomy
How you weigh risk before deciding
strong_signals: Explains why waiting was costly
Says clearly what you decided yourself
Names the risk and how you limited it

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a real failure with stakes. Explain why the plan seemed right at the time, the candidate's own part in what went wrong, and how quickly they noticed and responded. Show the concrete lesson and a later example where they applied it. Spotify says it trusts people to take thoughtful risks and learn from mistakes, so own it without blame. Pitfalls: a disguised success, or blaming others.

looking_for: Whether you own mistakes
What you learned and applied later
strong_signals: Explains why the plan seemed right at the time
Owns your part without blame
Gives a later example of the lesson

sample_questions.question: Tell me about some difficult feedback you received and what you did with it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Describe the feedback in substance and who gave it. Be honest about the first reaction, then show the steps taken to change. Give evidence the change lasted, such as a later result or the person noticing. Strong answers show the candidate asks for feedback, not only receives it. Pitfalls: feedback that is really praise, or no visible change.

looking_for: How you take and act on hard feedback
Whether you seek feedback yourself
strong_signals: Describes the feedback in substance
Shows evidence the change stuck

sample_questions.question: Describe a time you worked to a tight deadline. How did you manage it?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Give the deadline, why it mattered and what made it hard. Show how the candidate cut scope, set priorities, and told stakeholders early about risks. Show action: what they started before everything was clear and which blockers they removed. Quantify the result and what was traded off. Pitfalls: only working longer hours, or hiding a slip until the end.

looking_for: How you deliver under time pressure
Whether you cut scope and communicate early
strong_signals: Names what was cut and why
Flags risk to stakeholders early
Quantifies the result
watch_outs: Hiding a slip until the end

sample_questions.question: What do you do to keep your ego in check when working in a team?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Answer with a real example, not a slogan. Show the candidate changing their mind when a teammate had a better idea, sharing credit, or helping another person succeed at a cost to their own work. Explain habits such as asking for review early and sharing context openly. Pitfalls: claiming to have no ego, or an example where the candidate was right all along.

looking_for: Whether you put the team ahead of being right
How you share credit and context
strong_signals: Gives a real example of changing your mind
Names habits like asking for review early
watch_outs: An example where you were right all along

sample_questions.question: Why Spotify, and why are you looking to leave your current role?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Be specific: link a Spotify product, technical problem or mission (connecting creators and listeners) to the candidate's past work and goals. Show they use the product and have a view on it. Explain the move in positive terms, about what they want next, not what they dislike now. Pitfalls: generic praise, only brand or pay, or criticizing the current employer.

looking_for: Whether you know what Spotify builds
What you want next in your career
strong_signals: Links a Spotify product or problem to your past work
Has a view on the product as a user

sample_questions.question: Tell me about a project you are proud of. How did you deliver it from start to finish?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick a project with scope that fits the target level and that the candidate clearly drove. Cover the goal, their own role, the hardest decisions and trade-offs, and how it shipped. Quantify the outcome for users or the business, and say what they would change. Spotify says it looks at the thinking behind the result, so explain the reasoning. Pitfalls: a team win with unclear personal part, or effort with no outcome.

looking_for: The scope of work you clearly drove
The thinking behind your result
strong_signals: Explains the hardest decisions and trade-offs
Quantifies the outcome
Scope fits the target level

sample_questions.question: Design an audio streaming service for about 100 million users.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify scope: on-demand tracks, offline, regions, start-up latency target. Split the catalog and metadata service from audio delivery. Store encoded files in object storage and serve them through a CDN, with several bitrates and adaptive switching. Cover prefetching the next track, licensing checks at play time, and logging play events through a stream for royalties and recommendations. Estimate load roughly and discuss hot tracks and failures. Pitfalls: serving audio from app servers, or ignoring start-up latency.

looking_for: How you separate metadata from audio delivery
Whether you plan for start-up latency and scale
strong_signals: Uses a CDN with several bitrates
Prefetches the next track
Logs play events through a stream

sample_questions.question: How would you design a weekly personalized playlist like Discover Weekly?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the goal (discovery of new tracks the user will like) and the refresh cadence. Describe offline batch generation: candidate retrieval from listening history and similar users or tracks, filtering already-heard and blocked items, ranking, and diversity rules. Store results per user and serve them cheaply. Cover cold start for new users and new tracks, and evaluation with saves, skips and repeat listens plus A/B tests. Pitfalls: computing it on each request, or no evaluation plan.

looking_for: How you split offline generation from serving
How you judge if recommendations are good
strong_signals: Separates retrieval, filtering and ranking
Handles cold start
Evaluates with saves, skips and A/B tests
watch_outs: Computing the playlist on each request

sample_questions.question: Design a feature that lets a user add a custom picture to a playlist. Anyone can view it, but only the owner can change it.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify size limits, moderation and how many playlists. Upload through a signed URL to object storage, process into several sizes, and store a reference in the playlist metadata. Enforce ownership on the write API, not the client. Serve images through a CDN with cache keys that change when the image changes. Cover content moderation, failed uploads and abuse. Pitfalls: storing images in the database, or checking permissions only in the app.

looking_for: How you handle uploads and permissions
Whether you think about caching and moderation
strong_signals: Uses object storage and a CDN
Enforces ownership on the server
Changes cache keys when the image changes
watch_outs: Permission checks only in the client

sample_questions.question: You are on call and a critical service goes down. Walk me through how you troubleshoot it and when you escalate.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start with impact: who is affected and how badly. Stabilize first (roll back a recent deploy, shift traffic, turn off a feature flag) before deep diagnosis. Use dashboards, logs and recent changes to form and test hypotheses. Communicate status on a regular rhythm and escalate early when impact is large or the cause is outside one's area. Afterwards, run a blameless review with follow-up actions. Pitfalls: debugging silently for an hour, or no rollback plan.

looking_for: How you triage and stabilize under pressure
When and how you escalate
strong_signals: Mitigates first, for example with a rollback
Tests hypotheses with logs and recent changes
Runs a blameless review afterwards
watch_outs: Debugging silently for a long time

sample_questions.question: How would you use machine learning to find duplicate songs in a large catalog?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Define duplicate first: the same recording uploaded twice, remasters, live versions or covers. Combine metadata signals (title, artist, duration, ISRC codes) with audio fingerprints or embeddings. Use blocking or approximate nearest neighbor search to avoid comparing every pair, then a classifier on pair features. Build labels from known matches and human review, and measure precision and recall, with a high precision bar before merging. Pitfalls: comparing all pairs, or treating covers as duplicates.

looking_for: How you define the problem before modeling
How you scale matching and measure it
strong_signals: Defines what counts as a duplicate
Combines metadata and audio signals
Uses blocking or nearest neighbor search

sample_questions.question: How would you handle the cold-start problem for brand-new users in a music recommendation system?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Use what is known at sign-up: country, device, language, and a short taste picker. Start with popular and regional content, then learn fast from early plays, skips and saves, with more exploration at first. Use content-based features so new tracks and artists can also be recommended. Measure early retention and satisfaction for new users separately. Pitfalls: only showing global top charts, or waiting weeks for enough data.

looking_for: How you recommend with little data
How fast you learn from early signals
strong_signals: Uses sign-up context and a taste picker
Explores more at first, then exploits
Measures new-user retention separately

sample_questions.question: How would you measure the success of Discover Weekly?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Start from its goal: help listeners find new music they love. Pick a primary metric such as the share of users who save or repeatedly play a newly discovered track, with supporting metrics (weekly reach, tracks played per playlist, skip rate) and guardrails (overall listening time, artist diversity). Explain how to read changes through A/B tests and cohorts. Pitfalls: only counting playlist opens, or many metrics with no primary one.

looking_for: How you turn a product goal into metrics
Whether you choose one primary metric
strong_signals: Ties the metric to real discovery, like saves
Adds guardrails such as total listening
Explains how A/B tests read the change
watch_outs: Many metrics with no primary one

sample_questions.question: Spotify app installs dropped 25%. What happened, and what would you do?
sample_questions.strong_answer: Clarify the metric, the time window and whether the drop is sudden or gradual. Rule out tracking or data bugs. Segment by platform, app store, country, acquisition channel and device. Check internal changes (store listing, a release, marketing spend) and external ones (store policy, competitor launch, seasonality). Rank hypotheses, name the data that tests each, and propose actions, including fixing a broken channel. Pitfalls: guessing causes without structure, or skipping the data check.

looking_for: How you structure a metric investigation
Whether you rule out data issues first
strong_signals: Segments by platform, store, country and channel
Checks internal and external changes
Ranks hypotheses with the data to test each

sample_questions.question: How would you design an experiment to test a new shuffle algorithm?
sample_questions.strong_answer: State the hypothesis: users find the new shuffle more satisfying. Choose the unit (user, not session) and a primary metric such as skip rate or listening time in shuffle sessions, plus guardrails like overall listening and complaints. Size the test with power analysis, run it long enough to cover weekly patterns and novelty effects, and check segments such as playlist length. Say how the result decides the launch. Pitfalls: randomizing by session, or stopping as soon as it looks good.

looking_for: How you design a clean A/B test
How the result turns into a decision
strong_signals: Picks the user as the unit
Sets a primary metric and guardrails
Accounts for novelty and weekly patterns
watch_outs: Stopping early when it looks good

sample_questions.question: Design a collaborative listening feature, where friends listen together.
sample_questions.strong_answer: Pick one user group and situation (friends far apart, a party, a car trip) and their main pain. Explore a few solutions, then choose one and walk through the key flows: inviting, joining, who controls the queue, and what happens when someone leaves. Name the constraints (latency, licensing, free versus premium). Define success (sessions started and repeated) and guardrails. Pitfalls: jumping to screens before the user, or ignoring control conflicts in a group.

looking_for: Whether you start from a real user situation
How you handle group control and constraints
strong_signals: Picks one group and its main pain
Walks through invite, join and queue control
Defines success and guardrails
watch_outs: Jumping to screens before the user
Ignoring conflicts over who controls the music

bar_by_level.scope_expectation: Entry level. Delivers well-defined tasks inside one squad with guidance.
Early career. Delivers features in one squad with less guidance and writes readable, tested code.
Owns features within a squad from design to launch and works independently.
Owns systems for a squad, leads design work and mentors others. Loop leans more on system design.
Shapes architecture across several squads and influences technical decisions beyond own team.
Leads technical strategy across studios or a whole mission, unifies fragmented systems and brings other senior engineers along.
Owns a product area, its strategy and metrics, and leads a cross-functional team.
Owns analysis or models for a product area and uses data to change product decisions.
Leads design for a product area end to end and builds alignment across disciplines.

persona.tone: Friendly, relaxed and conversational; treats the interview as a two-way exchange
persona.pace: Moderate; one story or problem at a time, with room to think out loud
persona.pushback_style: Asks for the thinking behind a result, what the candidate personally decided, and what they would do differently; pushes on vague 'we' answers and on trade-offs
persona.closing_style: Leaves time for the candidate's questions and may end with a light question, such as what music they are listening to

case_style.notes: PM and data cases center on Spotify features: improving the product, measuring personalized playlists, diagnosing metric drops and designing A/B tests. Engineering case studies are real team problems such as incidents. Market sizing is rarely reported.

low_confidence_notes: values_framework: the three values (One Team, Human Judgment, Make It Happen) are from Spotify's current careers pages. 'Impact over activity' and 'Stay curious' are drawn from the same culture pages but are not among the three named values. The older five band values (Innovative, Collaborative, Sincere, Passionate, Playful) no longer appear on lifeatspotify.com; some prep guides still cite them.

loop_structure: Spotify's official page gives only recruiter screen, team interview and final round. Round names, durations and the PM, data and design loops come from prep sites, and the data and design loops mostly from CleverPrep, which may be partly generated. Loops vary by team.

bar_by_level: SWE level names (Associate Engineer to Staff Engineer) come from Levels.fyi URLs; Senior Staff Engineer from a Spotify job posting. Spotify has no public career ladder, so scope text is our summary. PM, data and design level names are generic job titles, not confirmed internal levels.
persona: inferred from Spotify's 'two-way exchange' wording and prep-site reports; no official description of interviewer style.
scoring_weights: our estimate from the qualities Spotify says it looks for (ownership, adaptability, collaboration, drive, the thinking behind results); no public source gives weights.
sample_questions: questions come from prep sites (Exponent/aced.io, Prepfully, techinterview.org, CleverPrep) that aggregate candidate reports; none are from Spotify itself.
